title: Why first-order LP methods suit a GPU: PDHG and PDLP

blocks.text: 11.4.1 Why First-Order LP Methods Suit a GPU: PDHG and PDLP

GridCap's analysts solve the LP relaxation of the capital plan many times a night: once per scenario, per region, per budget case. The relaxation is the plan with "fund it or not" loosened to "fund any share from 0 to 1" (lesson 3.1.1), and its optimum is an upper bound on what any real plan can be worth. A colleague asks whether a **GPU** (graphics processing unit: a card with thousands of small arithmetic cores that run the same instruction on many numbers at once) would make those solves faster. The answer depends on the algorithm. Simplex and interior point, the methods of lessons 2.2.2 and 2.4.1, spend their time solving systems of linear equations, and that work does not spread well over thousands of cores. A **first-order method** spends its time on matrix-vector products, and those do. This lesson shows the first-order method HiGHS, cuOpt and OR-Tools share, PDHG, on GridCap's numbers; what PDLP adds to it; and what it gives up: it stops at a tolerance, not at a vertex. GridCap is a fictional utility; its numbers are teaching data.
Lesson 2.4.1 met PDHG on a two-variable LP with rows of the form $`Ax \le b`$. Here the rows are GridCap's, some of them equalities, and the program runs on the matrix as a whole.
The Model
The LP relaxation of GridCap small's start-year model (lesson 6.4.1, without its parent-child rows), built by `lps.gridcap_timing("small")`:

**Sets.** $`P`$ the 40 projects; $`Y`$ the years 2027 to 2031; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$ the years project $`i`$ may start in; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups.

**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$, the NPV of project $`i`$ started in year $`t`$ ($k); $`s_{i,t,y}`$, what project $`i`$ started in $`t`$ spends in year $`y`$ ($k); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`0 \le x_{i,t} \le 1`$ for every $`i \in P`$, $`t \in T_i`$: the share of project $`i`$ started in year $`t`$ (80 variables).
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**
The code names each row by its label: `once_P001`, `must_P003`, `alt_G001`, `budget_2029`. The 47 rows and 80 columns hold 204 nonzero coefficients.

The module's programs keep a model as a plain dict (objective, rows in compressed sparse row form, row bounds, variable bounds), so HiGHS, OR-Tools' PDLP and cuOpt all read the same numbers. In that form every row is two-sided: $`\ell^c_r \le a_r x \le u^c_r`$, with $`\ell^c_r = -\infty`$ for a $`\le`$ row and $`\ell^c_r = u^c_r = 1`$ for a must row.
Every LP Is a Saddle Point: the Plan Maximises, the Prices Minimise

Write the model as $`\max c^\top x`$ subject to $`\ell^c \le Ax \le u^c`$ and $`\ell \le x \le u`$. Give each row $`r`$ one price $`y_r`$ of any sign: $`y_r > 0`$ prices the row's upper side ($`a_r x \le u^c_r`$), $`y_r < 0`$ its lower side. With $`[y]_+ = \max(y, 0)`$ and $`[y]_- = \max(-y, 0)`$, the **Lagrangian** is
L(x, y) = c^\top x - y^\top A x + \sum_r \bigl( u^c_r\,[y_r]_+ - \ell^c_r\,[y_r]_- \bigr)

For a price $`y_r \ge 0`$ the row's term is $`y_r (u^c_r - a_r x)`$, its slack valued at the price, exactly lesson 2.4.1's $`y^\top (b - Ax)`$. For $`y_r \le 0`$ it is $`|y_r| (a_r x - \ell^c_r)`$, the slack above the lower side. A row with no lower side ($`\ell^c_r = -\infty`$) can only take a price $`y_r \ge 0`$, and a row with no upper side only $`y_r \le 0`$.
The optimal plan and the optimal prices form a **saddle point** of $`L`$:
\max_{\ell \le x \le u} \; \min_{y} \; L(x, y)

The plan $`x`$ makes $`L`$ as large as it can, the prices make it as small as they can, and at the saddle point neither can gain by moving alone. The inner minimum is $`c^\top x`$ when $`x`$ keeps every row (the best price on a kept row is 0) and $`-\infty`$ when it breaks one, so the outer maximum is the LP. The OR-Tools PDLP documentation writes the same problem with a minimisation outside, the objective's sign flipped, and $`K = -A`$; the content is the same.
A PDHG Iteration Is Two Matrix-Vector Products and Two Clips
**PDHG**, the primal-dual hybrid gradient method, moves the plan up its gradient and the prices down theirs, in turn. With step sizes $`\tau, \sigma > 0`$, one iteration is

The first line is lesson 2.4.1's primal step: $`c - A^\top y`$ is each variable's reduced cost at prices $`y`$, and the clip puts each variable back between its bounds. The second and third lines are the dual step at the look-ahead point $`2x^{k+1} - x^k`$. The third line is the clip for a two-sided row: if the plan overshoots the upper side, the first term raises the upper price; if it falls below the lower side, the second term makes the price negative; if it sits between, both terms shrink toward 0. When $`\ell^c_r = -\infty`$ the second term is always 0, and the line becomes 2.4.1's $`\max(0, \cdot)`$. `pdhg_gridcap.py` writes it with NumPy and SciPy, on the whole matrix:

x_new = np.clip(x + tau * (c - A.T @ y), lo, hi)                          # primal: up the gradient, clip
        v = y + sigma * (A @ (2 * x_new - x))                                      # dual: at the look-ahead point
        y = np.maximum(0.0, v - sigma * row_hi) + np.minimum(0.0, v - sigma * row_lo)   # clip by the row's sides
        x = x_new

A: 47 x 80, 204 nonzeros, entries from 1 to 5680; simplex optimum 26,587.4415
work per iteration: 2 x 204 multiply-adds for A x and A'y, plus 127 clips; no factorization

Constant steps converge when $`\tau \sigma \lVert A \rVert_2^2 \le 1`$, where $`\lVert A \rVert_2`$ is the matrix's largest singular value (the PDLP paper cites this condition). The program uses $`\tau = \sigma = 0.9 / \lVert A \rVert_F`$; the Frobenius norm (the square root of the sum of all squared entries) is never smaller than $`\lVert A \rVert_2`$, so the condition holds.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Those Products Are What a GPU Does Best

An iteration reads each nonzero of $`A`$ twice, once for $`A x`$ and once for $`A^\top y`$, and then clips two vectors element by element. Every row of $`A x`$ is a separate sum that needs nothing from the other rows, and every clip is separate too. That is the shape of work a GPU is built for: thousands of cores each take a few rows, with no core waiting for another, and the speed is set by how fast the card's memory streams the matrix past them. PDHG never solves for the prices exactly: each iteration moves them by one dual step (the second and third lines of the iteration above), and the next iteration starts from there.

Simplex and interior point do different work. A simplex iteration solves linear systems with the current basis, and an interior point iteration solves one with a matrix built from $`A`$ and the current point (lesson 2.4.1). Both **factorize** a matrix (split it into triangular factors, the LU or Cholesky factorization), and a factorization is a chain of steps where each one needs the ones before it, and it can fill zero entries with nonzeros, so it needs more memory than $`A`$. That chain does not split cleanly into thousands of independent pieces. A first-order method never factorizes anything: it needs memory for $`A`$ and a few vectors, and nothing else. The PDLP paper gives this as the reason it scales, since its core operation is the matrix-vector product, and the cuPDLP papers built GPU versions on it (lesson 11.4.3 measures two of them).
Plain PDHG Stalls on GridCap's Numbers; Rescaling Rescues It
The bare iteration above, run 100,000 times on GridCap small, and then again after rescaling the rows and columns:

As built, the method is stuck: after 100,000 iterations the plan is 13% above the optimum and still breaks a row by 3.0. The reason is in the first output line: the entries of $`A`$ run from 1 (the once and must rows) to 5,680 (a budget row). The step sizes must suit the largest entries, so they are tiny ($`4.66 \times 10^{-5}`$). A price moves by $`\sigma`$ times its row's breach per iteration, about $`1.4 \times 10^{-4}`$ for the breach of 3.0 in the table, so the prices crawl and the plan with them. After rescaling the steps are 1,500 times larger. Raising the steps that far by hand is no cure: with the entries as built, steps 1,500 times larger break the convergence condition above many times over. Rescaling shrinks the large entries, so that the condition itself allows the larger steps.

**Rescaling** (also called **diagonal preconditioning**) fixes the units. It multiplies row $`j`$ by a number $`r_j`$ and column $`i`$ by a number $`s_i`$, so that the rescaled matrix is $`\operatorname{diag}(r)\, A \, \operatorname{diag}(s)`$ and every row's and column's largest entry is near 1, solves the rescaled LP for $`x' = x / s`$, and maps the answer back. The Ruiz method does it by repeatedly dividing by the square root of each row's and column's largest entry:

def ruiz(A, rounds: int = 10):
    """Row and column scalings r, s that bring every row's and column's largest |entry| near 1."""
    r, s = np.ones(A.shape[0]), np.ones(A.shape[1])
    for _ in range(rounds):
        B = scipy.sparse.diags(r) @ A @ scipy.sparse.diags(s)
        r /= np.sqrt(abs(B).max(axis=1).toarray().ravel())
        s /= np.sqrt(abs(B).max(axis=0).toarray().ravel())
    return r, s
rescaled: entries from 0.24 to 1.00

The same iteration on the rescaled LP reaches a relative error of $`4.2 \times 10^{-4}`$ in 1,000 iterations and $`4.8 \times 10^{-6}`$ in 100,000. Rescaling changes the units, not the LP: the plan mapped back is a plan of the original model, and the row bounds and objective scale with it. It is still slow, and it wanders (at 10,000 iterations the violation is back up to 2.9), which is what PDLP's other additions are for.
PDLP Adds Restarts, Rescaling, Adaptive Steps and a Primal Weight

**PDLP** (primal-dual hybrid gradient for LP) is PDHG with enhancements that make it practical. The PDLP paper names diagonal preconditioning, presolving, adaptive step sizes and adaptive restarting, and its algorithm also updates a primal weight. OR-Tools' parameters (`PrimalDualHybridGradientParams` in `solvers.proto`) let you switch each one off:

items: **Rescaling.** Ruiz rescaling (`l_inf_ruiz_iterations`, 5 rounds by default) and then a rescaling by the rows' and columns' 2-norms (`l2_norm_rescaling`, on), as in the section above.

**Adaptive restarts** (`restart_strategy`, `ADAPTIVE_HEURISTIC`). PDHG's average of recent iterates is often closer to the optimum than its last iterate, but averaging over a long run slows it down. PDLP periodically restarts the method from the better of the two, judged by a measure of distance from optimality, which keeps the progress and drops the slow tail.

**Adaptive step sizes** (`linesearch_rule`, `ADAPTIVE_LINESEARCH_RULE`). Instead of the safe but pessimistic $`0.9 / \lVert A \rVert`$, PDLP tries a larger step, checks a condition from the convergence theory, and reduces it and tries again only if the step fails it.

**Primal weight** $`\omega`$ (`primal_weight_update_smoothing`). The steps are $`\tau = \eta / \omega`$ and $`\sigma = \eta\,\omega`$, so $`\omega`$ trades how far the plan moves against how far the prices move. PDLP starts it from the ratio of the objective's norm to the bounds' norm and updates it at each restart, so that neither side lags.
**Presolve** (`presolve_options.use_glop`, off by default in OR-Tools): simplifications before the method starts.

blocks.text: `pdlp_gridcap.py` solves GridCap small with OR-Tools' PDLP through its direct API (the one OR-Tools' `simple_pdlp_program.py` sample uses), once with the defaults and once with each feature switched off:

features = {
        "PDLP defaults": {},
        "no restarts": {"restart_strategy": solvers_pb2.PrimalDualHybridGradientParams.NO_RESTARTS},
        "no rescaling": {"l_inf_ruiz_iterations": 0, "l2_norm_rescaling": False},
        "constant step size": {"linesearch_rule": solvers_pb2.PrimalDualHybridGradientParams.CONSTANT_STEP_SIZE_RULE},
        "fixed primal weight": {"primal_weight_update_smoothing": 0.0},
    }

What PDLP adds to plain PDHG: iterations to 1e-6 with one feature switched off (limit 100,000)
PDLP defaults            576 iterations  OPTIMAL
no restarts             7616 iterations  OPTIMAL
no rescaling          100000 iterations  ITERATION_LIMIT
constant step size      1024 iterations  OPTIMAL
fixed primal weight      640 iterations  OPTIMAL

With everything on, PDLP reaches the tolerance in 576 iterations, against the 100,000 that plain PDHG did not finish. Each feature's share, on this model: without rescaling it does not finish either (the stall of the section above); without restarts it needs 13 times the iterations; a constant step needs 1.8 times; a frozen primal weight costs 11% more. These are one model's numbers; the PDLP paper measures each feature over hundreds of LPs.
None of these features adds a factorization. Each iteration is still matrix-vector products and clips, plus a few vector norms, so PDLP keeps the property that puts it on a GPU.
A First-Order Method Stops at a Tolerance, Not at a Vertex

Simplex ends on a **vertex** with a **basis**: an exact corner of the feasible region, with the list of variables that define it (lessons 2.2.1 and 2.2.2). PDLP has neither. It stops when its point is close enough, by three measures from the PDLP paper, each relative to the size of the data:
OR-Tools sets $`\varepsilon`$ in `simple_optimality_criteria` (both the relative and the absolute part default to $`10^{-6}`$); `ortools_pdlp` in `lps.py` sets both to the tolerance it is given:

criteria = params.termination_criteria.simple_optimality_criteria
    criteria.eps_optimal_relative = eps
    criteria.eps_optimal_absolute = eps

HiGHS simplex (CPU): Optimal, objective 26587.441510, 25 iterations, 72 of 80 values exactly 0 or 1

PDLP (CPU, 1 thread): where it stops is set by the tolerance
tolerance  iterations   objective      rel. error  max violation  values exactly 0 or 1
    1e-02          64    26607.7410     7.6e-04        2.6e+01                     69
    1e-04         192    26587.6557     8.1e-06        1.4e-01                     69
    1e-06         576    26587.4632     8.2e-07        1.2e-02                     70
    1e-08         896    26587.4413     8.7e-09        6.3e-08                     70
Read it row by row:

items: **The tolerance sets the cost.** Each factor of 100 in accuracy costs more iterations: 64, 192, 576, 896. The answer is as accurate as asked and no more.
**The relative error tracks the tolerance.** At every row the objective is within the tolerance of the simplex optimum, relatively.

**"Optimal" allows broken rows.** At $`10^{-6}`$ the plan breaks a row by 0.012, in $k. That is allowed: the primal measure compares the breach with the size of all the row bounds together, and GridCap's budgets run to thousands. A planner who reads "optimal" as "keeps every budget to the dollar" is wrong at every tolerance above. At $`10^{-8}`$ the breach is $`6.3 \times 10^{-8}`$.

**It is not the vertex.** Simplex ends with 72 of the 80 values exactly 0 or 1; PDLP, even at $`10^{-8}`$, has 70. Its point is near the optimal face, not on its corner, and it returns no basis. A model that needs a basis (for the warm starts of lesson 4.3.3, or for sensitivity ranges read from it) needs a simplex solve, or a crossover step that some solvers run after PDLP to move to a vertex.

blocks.text: The trace shows how it gets there:

The primal and dual objectives close in on each other from both sides, but not steadily: the primal residual (how far the rows are broken) falls to $`5.2 \times 10^{-4}`$ at iteration 256 and rises to 0.85 at 320. The residuals are not monotone, which is why PDLP checks all three measures together, and why "how many iterations" has no answer before the run.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **Every LP is a saddle point: the plan maximises, the prices minimise.** One price per row, of either sign for a two-sided row; at the saddle point neither side gains by moving.
**A PDHG iteration is two matrix-vector products and two clips.** The dual clip for a two-sided row is $`\max(0, v - \sigma u^c) + \min(0, v - \sigma \ell^c)`$.
**Those products are what a GPU does best.** Each row's sum is independent, and there is no factorization to chain the work or fill the memory.
**Plain PDHG stalls on GridCap's numbers; rescaling rescues it.** As built, 13% off after 100,000 iterations; rescaled, $`4.8 \times 10^{-6}`$.
**PDLP adds restarts, rescaling, adaptive steps and a primal weight.** 576 iterations to $`10^{-6}`$ with all of them; without rescaling, not done in 100,000.
**A first-order method stops at a tolerance, not at a vertex.** Relative criteria on the gap and the two residuals; rows broken by up to 0.012 at $`10^{-6}`$; no basis.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: a method whose steps use only gradients (here: products with $`A`$ and $`A^\top`$), never a factorization
primal-dual hybrid gradient: a primal step up $`c - A^\top y`$, a dual step at $`2x^{k+1} - x^k`$, each clipped
PDHG with rescaling, adaptive restarts, adaptive steps, a primal weight and optional presolve
the relative accuracy at which PDLP stops: gap, primal and dual residuals

blocks.text: **Further reading:** OR-Tools, [PDLP: the math](https://developers.google.com/optimization/lp/pdlp_math) (the primal and dual problems, the saddle-point form with $`K = -A`$, rescaling by diagonal matrices); the OR-Tools sample [`simple_pdlp_program.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/pdlp/samples/simple_pdlp_program.py) (the direct PDLP API this lesson's `ortools_pdlp` uses); the parameter comments in [`solvers.proto`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/pdlp/solvers.proto) (restart strategies, line search rules, Ruiz and 2-norm rescaling, the primal weight, termination criteria and their defaults); Applegate et al., [Practical Large-Scale Linear Programming using Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.04756) (the PDLP paper: the saddle point and PDHG update, the step condition, adaptive steps and restarts, primal weight, Ruiz and Pock-Chambolle preconditioning, the termination criteria, and the matrix-vector product as the reason PDLP scales).
Challenges

items: In `pdhg_gridcap.py`, change the equal steps to $`\tau = 0.9 / (\omega \lVert A \rVert_F)`$ and $`\sigma = 0.9\,\omega / \lVert A \rVert_F`$ with $`\omega = 0.1`$ and with $`\omega = 10`$ on the rescaled LP. Predict which converges faster, and why the primal weight is a ratio.
Switch off two PDLP features at once in `pdlp_gridcap.py`, restarts and adaptive steps. Predict whether the iterations multiply (13 × 1.8) or not.
A planner asks for "the LP bound to the dollar" from PDLP. Which tolerance would you set, and what would you tell them about the 47 rows?

blocks.text: Design Note: One Model Format for Every Solver

Every program of this module builds its model once, as a dict of plain lists, and hands the same numbers to HiGHS, to OR-Tools' PDLP (through SciPy's sparse matrices) and to cuOpt (as JSON, in a separate process). A comparison between solvers is then a comparison between algorithms and devices, never between two model builders that might disagree on a row. `violation` checks any solver's answer against those same lists, so no solver grades its own work.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change. Both run on the CPU, with or without a GPU.

**pdhg_gridcap.py.** Plain PDHG on GridCap small's LP relaxation, as built and after Ruiz rescaling (*A PDHG Iteration*, *Plain PDHG Stalls*). *Try:* Change `rounds` in `ruiz` from 10 to 1 and predict the relative error after 1,000 iterations.

**pdlp_gridcap.py.** OR-Tools' PDLP on the same LP at four tolerances, its trace, and each feature switched off (*PDLP Adds*, *A First-Order Method Stops at a Tolerance*). *Try:* Turn on `presolve_options.use_glop` through `tweaks` and predict whether the iterations to $`10^{-6}`$ change.
